sections.title: The Mitzva to Love Converts
sections.html:
There is a great mitzva incumbent upon all of Israel to love the convert (ger) who comes to join the people of Israel and its destiny of bringing blessing to all the families of the earth. For in addition to the mitzva "You shall love your fellow as yourself" (Vayikra 19:18), which includes all of Israel, converts among them, the Torah added a special mitzva to love the convert, as it is stated (Devarim 10:19): "You shall love the stranger (ger), for you were strangers in the land of Egypt." And it is stated (Vayikra 19:34): "The stranger who dwells with you shall be to you as a native among you, and you shall love him as yourself, for you were strangers in the land of Egypt; I am the Lord your God." Thus, by loving the convert one fulfills two positive Torah commandments. Love is not expressed only in the feelings of the heart, but also in speech and in deed, for one who loves his fellow speaks in his praise and is protective of his honor and his property just as he is protective of his own honor and his own property (Rambam, Hilkhot De'ot 6:3-4).

God, too, loves converts with an especially great love, as it is stated (Devarim 10:17-18): "For the Lord your God, He is God of gods and Lord of lords, the great, mighty and awesome God … and He loves the stranger, giving him bread and clothing." The Sages said: The convert is more beloved than Israel, for had Israel not stood at Mount Sinai and seen the thunder, the torches, the lightning and the smoking mountain, they would not have accepted upon themselves the yoke of the kingship of Heaven; whereas this convert saw none of these, yet he accepted upon himself the yoke of the kingship of Heaven and came to complete himself and to draw close to God – is there anything more beloved than this?! (Tanḥuma, Lekh Lekha 6). The stature of converts is greater than the stature of the righteous who love God, for of the righteous it is stated (Shofetim 5:31): "And those who love Him are like the sun going forth in its might," whereas converts are on a still higher level, for God loves them! As Rabbi Shimon bar Yoḥai said: "Who is greater – one who loves the king, or one whom the king loves? Say: one whom the king loves! Therefore it is stated: 'and He loves the stranger, giving him bread and clothing'" (Mekhilta on Shemot 22:20).

The Sages further said (Bemidbar Rabba 8:2): A parable – to what may the matter be compared? To a king who had a flock, and every day the flock would go out to the field and return in the evening. Once, a deer entered among the flock and went along with the goats. The deer would go out to graze with them and return with them. They said to the king: This deer accompanies your flock and grazes with them every single day. The king loved it greatly, and instructed the shepherds not to scold it or strike it, and to see to it that it drank and ate. The shepherds said to the king: You have so many he-goats and sheep, goats and kids – why do you love this deer more than all of them? The king said to them: The flock, whether it wishes or not, this is its way – to graze in the field all day and in the evening to come and sleep inside the pen. But deer sleep in the wilderness; it is not their way to enter places of human settlement. Shall we not be grateful to this one, which left the whole wide, great wilderness, the place of all the wild animals, and came and stayed in the courtyard?! So too must we be grateful to the convert, who left his family, his father's house, his nation and all the nations of the world, and came to us. Therefore God commanded many times regarding love of the convert, and warned not to cause him distress.

The Sages further said (Yalkut Shimoni 645): "The Holy One, blessed be He, said: How much I toiled over Israel! I brought them out of Egypt and gave light before them, I brought down the manna for them, I drove the quail to them, I brought up the well for them, I surrounded them with the clouds of glory – until they accepted My Torah; but this one came of his own accord, therefore he is as dear to Me as Israel and as a Levite." Moreover, because he abandoned his idols and came to cleave to God, one should love him. "The Holy One, blessed be He, said: It is enough that he left idolatry and came to you; I warn you to love him, for I love him," as it is stated (Devarim 10:18-19): "And He loves the stranger, giving him bread and clothing. You shall love the stranger, for you were strangers in the land of Egypt" (Tanḥuma, Vayikra 2). Continuing this, when the Sages formulated the text of the Amida prayer, they added 'the righteous converts' (gerei ha-tzedek) to the blessing concerning the righteous, so that by mentioning them in prayer Israel would fulfill the mitzva of loving the convert every day (R. Yehuda ben Yakar and Abudarham).

sections.title: The Prohibition of Wronging the Convert
sections.html:
All of Israel must take care not to cause one another distress. This prohibition is called the prohibition of 'ona'a' (wronging), and it includes two components: ona'at devarim (verbal wronging), not to cause distress through speech; and ona'at mamon (monetary wronging), not to cause distress by harming someone's property. The Torah added two more separate warnings not to cause distress to the convert, to teach us that anyone who causes him distress with words or with money transgresses three prohibitions (Bava Metzia 59b).

Regarding verbal wronging, the first prohibition is the prohibition against causing distress to any Jew, as it is stated (Vayikra 25:17): "You shall not wrong one another, and you shall fear your God, for I am the Lord your God." The second and third are specific to converts, as it is stated (Shemot 22:20): "You shall not wrong a stranger nor oppress him, for you were strangers in the land of Egypt." And it is stated (Vayikra 19:33-34): "When a stranger dwells with you in your land, you shall not wrong him. The stranger who dwells with you shall be to you as a native among you, and you shall love him as yourself, for you were strangers in the land of Egypt; I am the Lord your God." An example of wronging a convert (Bava Metzia 58b): "If he was a convert and came to study Torah, one should not say to him: 'Shall a mouth that ate carcasses and torn animals, abominations and creeping things, come to study the Torah that was spoken from the mouth of the Almighty?!'" The children of converts are also included in the prohibition of wronging the convert (Mishna, ibid.): "If he is the son of converts, one should not say to him: 'Remember the deeds of your ancestors.'"

Likewise regarding monetary wronging, it is stated concerning all of Israel (Shemot 22:24): "You shall not be to him as a creditor" – that is, if he took a loan and is unable to repay, you shall not press him over it. Likewise, when conducting business, it is forbidden to deceive another and thereby cause him distress, as it is stated (Vayikra 25:14): "And if you sell something to your fellow or buy from the hand of your fellow – you shall not wrong one another." The Torah added two more special prohibitions regarding monetary wronging of the convert, as it is stated (Shemot 22:20): "You shall not wrong a stranger nor oppress him, for you were strangers in the land of Egypt" – and "nor oppress him" refers to monetary wronging. And it is further stated (Shemot 23:9): "You shall not oppress a stranger, for you know the soul of the stranger, since you were strangers in the land of Egypt." Just as Israel suffered from the oppression "with which the Egyptians oppress them" (Shemot 3:9), so they were warned not to oppress converts.

There is also a special warning to judges not to exploit the convert's weakness and pervert his judgment, as it is stated (Devarim 24:17-18): "You shall not pervert the judgment of the stranger or the orphan … and you shall remember that you were a slave in Egypt and the Lord your God redeemed you from there; therefore I command you to do this thing" (and likewise in Shemot 23:6-9). To strengthen Israel in this, we were warned about it in a special way at the ceremony of the blessing and the curse, as it is stated (Devarim 27:19): "Cursed is he who perverts the judgment of the stranger, the orphan and the widow; and all the people shall say: Amen."

The Torah likewise added a warning not to exploit the convert's weakness and defraud him of his wages, as it is stated (ibid. 24:14): "You shall not defraud a hired worker who is poor and needy, whether of your brothers or of your strangers who are in your land, within your gates."

On the one hand, monetary wronging is more severe, since loss of money can lead to hunger, illness and death. On the other hand, there are aspects in which verbal wronging is more severe. First, monetary prohibitions are clear and evident, and the courts enforce them, so most people are accustomed to being careful about them. Verbal wronging, however, is a matter of the heart, and the sinner can claim that he did not intend to insult; therefore the Torah warned: "and you shall fear your God." Second, in a certain respect verbal wronging is more severe, as the Sages said (Bava Metzia 58b), for it harms the soul, whereas in monetary wronging only property is harmed. In addition, money taken unlawfully can be returned, and then, once the financial pressure passes, the distress will be forgotten. But verbal wronging is harder to undo and repair, for the distress and the insult may remain in the heart for many years.

To help the convert overcome the difficulties that accompany his absorption, and to save Jews from sinning by exploiting his weakness or by hurting him inadvertently, the Torah repeatedly warned many times to treat converts with respect and love and not to cause them distress (Bava Metzia 59b). God even added protection upon their protection, as it is stated (Tehillim 146:9): "The Lord protects strangers" – "for He increased their protection so that they would not return to their former ways" (Bemidbar Rabba 8:2).

Since new immigrants (olim) also have similar difficulties, all the mitzvot Israel was commanded regarding converts apply also to the absorption of immigrants (Sefer Ha-ḥinukh 431).

sections.title: Respecting the Convert
sections.html:
For two reasons one must respect the convert and take care not to cause him distress. First, we must honor him for his decision to leave his family, his people, his country and his mother tongue and to join the people of Israel. Second, we must take extra care not to cause him distress, because now he is alone in an unfamiliar society, and any slight insult may undermine his confidence, distress him and sadden him. In his previous surroundings he knew how to behave as was customary and to earn respect, whereas now even a child knows how to observe the customs better than he does. Sometimes his pain and humiliation grow so great that he will regret his decision to convert and will want to return to his former ways. The Sages explained that the prohibition of wronging the convert was placed next to the prohibition of idolatry (Shemot 22:19-20) to teach us "that whoever wrongs a convert is as though he worships idols," for if one belittles him for having been an idol worshiper, the convert, out of his great humiliation, may return to his idolatry, and then the Jew will be responsible for this (Midrash Aggada, Buber ed., ibid.).

There is a need to warn specially about respecting the convert, because people tend to take pride in their origins and to look down on someone who comes from afar to join them. Therefore the Torah warned (Vayikra 19:33-34): "When a stranger dwells with you in your land – you shall not wrong him … and you shall love him as yourself, for you were strangers in the land of Egypt; I am the Lord your God." Just as Israel did not want to be insulted in Egypt for being strangers, and do not want to be insulted today for having once been strangers in Egypt, so must they take care not to insult the convert. "A blemish that is in you, do not mention to your fellow" (Bava Metzia 59b).

The warning about loving the convert is most needed when Israel dwell in their own land, as it is stated (Vayikra 19:33-34): "When a stranger dwells with you in your land – you shall not wrong him. The stranger who dwells with you shall be to you as a native among you, and you shall love him as yourself." For a Jew who lives in exile identifies with the convert who joins him, but when Jews live as masters in their own land, they are liable to look down on converts (Ha'amek Davar, ibid.). Moreover, the land was apportioned to Israel, and the converts are landless, and consequently their status is inferior; therefore one must be very careful to safeguard all their rights, to treat them with love and to help them with acts of kindness (Rav S. R. Hirsch, ibid.; see below, section 4).

Even when the convert's friends and neighbors try to treat him with respect and sensitivity, it is almost certain that at times they will inadvertently stumble and cause him distress, since they are not familiar with his sensitivities and with the culture in which he grew up. And sometimes, because he does not understand the language and the customs, he will mistakenly think that he was slighted, and will be hurt to the depths of his soul, and for long days he will keep the pain of his humiliation in his heart, and no one will know that he was hurt. Even if he is exceedingly righteous, it is almost impossible that his integration into Israel will pass without complications and insults, most of which stem from lack of understanding. Even Onkelos the convert, whose translation of the Torah has been studied in every generation, was at the beginning of his path offended by Rabbi Eliezer to the point that he almost returned to his former ways (below 2:7). And even regarding Yitro the Sages said (Sanhedrin 94a) that when Moshe told him about the plagues with which God struck Egypt, Yitro was pained for the Egyptians and all his flesh "became prickles upon prickles." This is the source of the common saying that one should be careful not to disparage, in the presence of a convert and his descendants up to ten generations, the nations to which he had been connected, since he may be pained and offended by it. To reduce as much as possible the occasions on which the convert is offended, knowingly or unknowingly, one must make a point of always treating him with great respect, so that he feels loved and accepted; this will help him overcome misunderstandings, and as a result he will be less offended and distressed.

It is a mitzva to treat with respect even converts who do not conduct themselves according to halakha; and even though from the outset it may not have been fitting to convert them, since they converted and joined Israel, it is a mitzva to act kindly toward them and to take care not to insult them or cause them distress. Just as when we were in Egypt, although we were sunk in the forty-nine gates of impurity, God loved us and redeemed us, so too when the convert sins, one must not estrange oneself from him; rather, it is a mitzva to draw him near. And just as a person who has an illness or a scab-like lesion on one of his limbs does not seek to cut it off, for it is part of him, so must one treat converts even when they do not behave properly, as it is stated (Vayikra 19:34): "and you shall love him as yourself" (Ha'amek Davar, ibid.). And so we find that when King Shaul harmed the Gibonim, whose conversion was by deceit, he was punished severely for it, to teach all of Israel and the whole world how grave it is to harm converts (below 3:7).1

sections.title: The Mitzva to Gladden the Convert and Care for His Welfare
sections.html:
It is a mitzva for a person, at the time of his rejoicing, to include the converts, the poor, the orphans and the widows in his neighborhood, as it is stated (Devarim 16:14): "And you shall rejoice in your festival, you and your son and your daughter, your manservant and your maidservant, and the Levite, the stranger, the orphan and the widow who are within your gates." And so it is ruled in the Shulḥan Arukh (SA OḤ 529:2): "A person is obligated to be joyful and glad of heart on the festival, he and his wife and his children and all who are attached to him … and he is obligated to feed the convert, the orphan and the widow along with other poor people."

Likewise, when a person rejoiced over his produce and went up to the Temple with first fruits (bikkurim) and second tithe (ma'aser sheni), there was a mitzva for him to include the Levites and the converts in his joy and to invite them to eat with him at his meal from the meat of the peace offerings and from the fruits of 'ma'aser sheni,' as it is stated (Devarim 26:11): "And you shall rejoice in all the good that the Lord your God has given you and your household, you and the Levite and the stranger who is in your midst."

Therefore, when a person has a joyous occasion, such as a brit mila, a bar mitzva, a bat mitzva or a wedding, and he is preparing the guest list, it is a mitzva for him to remember the converts and the new immigrants, and to invite them respectfully to his celebration, thereby giving them a sense of belonging and security and gladdening them. Almost all converts and immigrants go through difficult periods in which it seems to them that nothing is working out: making a living is hard, they have no friends, their health is affected too, and they have to vacate the apartment and do not yet know where they will move. And when night falls, they remember the family and friends they left behind in order to realize a great vision, and their heart is bitter. And when they are invited to celebrations and see that members of the long-established families want their company and receive them with love, they feel wanted, and that their choice was justified, and they come back to believing that all the great hopes for which they converted will be realized. Presumably all those invited to the meal rejoice in it, but many times the converts and immigrants will be the most joyful of all, and thanks to them the joy will rise to the highest level of the joy of a mitzva. They will still need to cope with difficulties, but the sense of security and joy will give them the strength to withstand them.

Beyond including converts in one's joy, one must help them. For converts had no inheritance in the land, and being new, many times their livelihood was not settled either; therefore many of them were poor, and the gifts to the poor were intended for them as well, as it is stated (ibid. 24:19-22): "When you reap your harvest in your field and forget a sheaf in the field – you shall not go back to take it; it shall be for the stranger, the orphan and the widow, so that the Lord your God may bless you in all the work of your hands. When you beat your olive tree – you shall not go over the boughs after you; it shall be for the stranger, the orphan and the widow. When you gather the grapes of your vineyard – you shall not glean after you; it shall be for the stranger, the orphan and the widow. And you shall remember that you were a slave in the land of Egypt; therefore I command you to do this thing."

The produce of 'ma'aser ani' (the poor man's tithe), which was given in a dignified manner, was also designated for the Levites, who received no inheritance in the land and were engaged in education, and together with them the convert, the orphan and the widow, as it is stated (Devarim 14:29): "And the Levite, because he has no portion or inheritance with you, and the stranger, the orphan and the widow who are within your gates, shall come and eat and be satisfied, so that the Lord your God may bless you in all the work of your hand that you do" (and likewise ibid. 26:12-13).

It should be noted that whenever the Torah deals with helping the poor, it mentions converts before orphans and widows, for since converts have no relatives, they are more alone. And since they have no land and also do not know the language and the customs, they are liable to have greater difficulty making a living.

In addition, if they are helped to integrate, they and their children will be able to stand on their own feet and later even help others; and the greatest mitzva of charity is to set a person on his feet, so that he can support himself by his own efforts (Vayikra 25:35; Rambam, Hilkhot Matanot Aniyim 10:7; SA YD 249:6).

sections.title: The Virtue of Choice
sections.html:
From the fact that the Torah made it possible to convert, we learn of the immense power God gave man to choose the good, to the point that a person from any nation and language can create himself anew and decide to convert, thereby entering the community of Israel and the covenant with God. Every nation is defined by a whole set of behavioral and cultural characteristics, and even if a member of one nation moves to another country and receives its citizenship, his identity is still determined by his language, accent, culture, habits and manners. For example, a member of the Russian nation cannot choose to be English; rather, as long as his original identity is evident in him, he is still considered Russian. Only after he internalizes English culture and its language, to the point that he no longer appears different from the English in his behavior and culture, will his identity change to an English identity. Until then he will be considered at most as having a dual identity, a member of his original nation and a member of the nation he wishes to join. Generally people change their identity over three generations, and if their skin color is different, the period is longer. But a convert who has joined Israel, even though his appearance, language and manners are different, is considered a Jew in every respect from the moment he converts, for it is the choice to enter into the covenant with God and into the destiny of bringing blessing to the world that is decisive. The power of the choice to convert stems from the Divine image in man, by virtue of which he can choose to bring about an essential and irreversible change in his identity, as if to create himself anew, and to convert (based on Maharal, Gevurot Hashem 42).2

So important is the possibility of converting that already when God made the covenant with Israel at Mount Sinai, He also made a covenant with the converts who would convert in the future, as it is stated (Devarim 29:13-14): "Not with you alone do I make this covenant and this oath, but with him who stands here with us today before the Lord our God, and with him who is not here with us today." Included in "him who is not here with us today" are "converts who will convert in the future" (Shevuot 39a). Thus from the very beginning, when God chose Israel, He opened a gate to all human beings, so that they could convert and join the great destiny of the people of Israel to bring blessing to all the families of the earth and to repair the world. The Sages further said (Keritot 9a) that it is impossible for there to be a generation in which converts are not accepted, as it is stated (Bemidbar 15:14): "And if a stranger dwells with you … throughout your generations."

The Sages said (Tanḥuma, Vayakhel 8) that this is why "the Torah was given in the wilderness, to say: Just as the wilderness is ownerless, open to all people, so too the words of Torah are open to whoever wishes to learn. So that a person should not say: I am a son of Torah, and the Torah was given to me and to my forefathers, whereas you and your forefathers were not sons of Torah, but rather your forefathers were converts. Therefore it is stated (Devarim 33:4): 'Moshe commanded us the Torah, an inheritance of the congregation of Yaakov' – for everyone who gathers into Yaakov; even converts who engage in Torah are equal to the High Priest." As it is stated (Vayikra 18:5): "You shall keep My statutes and My ordinances, which a person shall do and live by them; I am the Lord" – it does not say 'a Kohen, a Levite and an Israelite,' but rather 'a person.' Therefore, "there shall be one Torah and one ordinance for you and for the stranger who dwells with you" (Bemidbar 15:16). And so we find that from Yitro the convert came forth great Torah scholars who merited divine inspiration (ru'aḥ ha-kodesh), and they would sit in the Chamber of Hewn Stone, and all of Israel would hear halakha from their mouths. Likewise Shemaya and Avtalyon were descendants of Sisera, and they taught Torah in public like the Men of the Great Assembly [?]. Thus from the outset the Torah was given to Israel together with all the converts who would join them in the future.

Great is the virtue of the converts' choice, to the point that the Sages said (Mekhilta on Shemot 22:20) that they are beloved, and all the qualities stated regarding Israel were stated regarding them, as it is stated (Yeshayahu 56:3-8): "Let not the foreigner who has joined himself to the Lord say: The Lord will surely separate me from His people … For thus says the Lord … And the foreigners who join themselves to the Lord, to serve Him and to love the name of the Lord, to be His servants … I will bring them to My holy mountain and make them joyful in My house of prayer; their burnt offerings and their sacrifices shall be accepted upon My altar, for My house shall be called a house of prayer for all peoples. Thus says the Lord God, who gathers the dispersed of Israel: I will yet gather others to him, besides those already gathered." Thus converts, too, are called, like Israel, servants of God, ministers of God and lovers of God; they too are included in the covenant with God and are acceptable before Him, and the ingathering of the exiles includes all the converts who join Israel as well. Indeed, the Children of Israel themselves are called 'strangers' (gerim) in this world before God, as it is stated (Vayikra 25:23): "For you are strangers and sojourners with Me." And King David likewise called himself a stranger before God, as it is stated (I Divrei Ha-yamim 29:15): "For we are strangers before You."

sections.title: Segula and Choice
sections.html:
In Israel the quality of segula (innate, chosen distinctiveness) stands out. This is the natural quality in the soul of Israel: they are members of the people that God formed in order to reveal His light to the world, and by their nature they cleave to the Torah and wish to bring blessing to the world. Granted, every Jew needs to choose, but his choice rests on his being a member of the Jewish people continuing the heritage of the forefathers, and the question is whether he will be loyal to his people and strive to add his unique contribution to increasing the light of the Torah and its blessing in the world.

In converts, by contrast, the quality of choice stands out more, for there is no human decision that expresses the power of choice more than the choice to convert. Nevertheless, after the conversion it becomes clear that from the very beginning there was a holy Israelite spark at the root of his soul, by virtue of which he could be roused to choose to join the people of Israel and the covenant with God. As the Sages said (Shabbat 146a), the roots of the souls of converts stood at Mount Sinai; and just as through Israel's participation in the revelation at Mount Sinai the impurity (zuhama) that hinders cleaving to the Torah and overcoming the evil inclination ceased from them, so the impurity ceased from the root of the converts' souls, and by virtue of this segula-power in their souls they were able to convert.

It turns out that both in the Children of Israel and in converts there is a quality of segula and a quality of choice, except that in the Children of Israel segula stands out more, whereas in converts choice stands out more. For although converts have a root in Israel, they must choose to change their identity and join the people of Israel and the covenant with God. And even after the conversion, difficulties and trials will still confront them, in which they will need to strengthen themselves in their choice to bind themselves to the people of Israel and to the Torah, in order to add their unique contribution to revealing God's light and blessing in the world.

The Children of Israel are more connected to the Written Torah and to prophecy, in which the Divine aspect stands out more, and the segula of Israel is that they are capable of receiving the supreme Divine revelation. Converts, by contrast, are more connected to the Oral Torah, in which the aspect of innovation that stems from human choice is more revealed. Moshe our teacher, the greatest of the prophets, who received the Torah at Sinai, was of the most distinguished lineage in Israel, and likewise the prophets after him were mainly descendants of Israelites of distinguished lineage. In contrast, the inspiration that converts merit comes mainly from divine inspiration (ru'aḥ ha-kodesh), which is revealed through the efforts of study made out of choice. Thus Yitro, who converted, merited to innovate from his own understanding the order of judgment in Israel, in the manner of the Oral Torah. Likewise Rabbi Akiva, the greatest of the sages of the Oral Torah, was the son of Yosef the convert. Through combining the two forces together – of Israel and of converts, segula and choice, prophecy and divine inspiration, the Written Torah and the Oral Torah – the Torah is revealed in its full light, and Israel are able to bring blessing to all the nations and to repair the world under the kingship of the Almighty.3

sections.title: Rectifying the Sin of Adam Through Conversion
sections.html:
In the beginning God created the world lacking, and He created man in His image, in the image of God, so that he would be able to cleave to His ways, to repair the world and to perfect it, as it is stated (Bereishit 2:15): "And the Lord God took the man and placed him in the Garden of Eden, to work it and to guard it." "To work it" means to develop the world and perfect it; "to guard it" means to take care not to spoil it through sins. The Sages explained that God created man in such a way that diverse and varied qualities were hidden within him, and when he would be fruitful and multiply, he would divide into seventy nations, each of which has its own special qualities and traits, through which it can add a unique good to the world, and without it the world is lacking. And already at the time of Creation, God created the soul of Israel, so that over time it would be revealed in the people of Israel, whose destiny is to reveal faith in the One God, thereby drawing God's light and blessing into the world, and to help reveal and clarify the special virtue of each nation. Through this there will be peace among all the nations, such that the connection between the nations, the people and the talents will be a fruitful connection of empowerment and life, blessing and joy. Thus the central role of the people of Israel in relation to the nations is like that of the heart in relation to all the limbs of the body (Kuzari 2:36).

As a result of the sin of Adam, who ate from the Tree of Knowledge of good and evil, good and evil became intermingled within him, and the serpent cast an impurity (zuhama) of wickedness into Ḥava and all her offspring (Shabbat 146a); since then man's task has become more complex and complicated. Before the sin the distinction between good and evil was clear, and therefore it was easier to choose the good. But after the sin, evil dross clung to every good thing, and good sparks became intermingled in every evil thing. Values, too, became intermingled with one another, in such a way that they harm one another. As a result, the process of clarifying and refining values became long and complicated, and bound up with trials, failures, suffering and the learning of lessons.

The process of the emergence of the people of Israel also became longer and more complicated. Ten generations passed from Adam to Noaḥ, who established the faith that is revealed in proper conduct (derekh eretz) and in the settlement of the world. And another ten generations from Noaḥ to Avraham our father, who began to illuminate the world with the light of faith in God's unity. After that, in a process of three generations, the forefathers and foremothers purified themselves of the impurity of wickedness, until all the sons of Yaakov our father were called the Children of Israel, and were chosen to inherit the holy land and to draw faith and blessing into the world. And still the Children of Israel were not sufficiently purified to be worthy of entering into the covenant with God and receiving the Torah. For this they needed to go down to Egypt and be strangers in a land not their own, to experience all the wickedness in the world, and to understand the greatness of the destiny placed upon them – to cleave to the values of freedom, justice and morality, and to bring blessing to the world (see Kuzari 1:95).

That is to say, as a result of the sin of Adam and the intermingling of good with evil, the entire people of Israel required a process of refinement and conversion upon entering into the covenant with God. The process began with the Children of Israel being strangers in Egypt; it continued with their agreement to leave the forty-nine gates of impurity of Egyptian idolatrous culture, an agreement expressed through the brit mila, which strengthened their Israelite identity, and through the offering of the Pesaḥ sacrifice, which expressed denial of the idols of Egypt; and it concluded with the acceptance of the Torah and the mitzvot at the revelation at Mount Sinai and the declaration "We will do and we will hear" (Shemot 24:7). Similarly, when a gentile wishes to convert, he must decide to leave his own Egypt, that is, everything that enslaves his soul, to join the people of Israel and to accept the Torah and the mitzvot in order to bring blessing and redemption to himself and to the world. And the entire order of conversion follows the order of the conversion of the Children of Israel, as it is stated (Bemidbar 15:15): "As you are, so shall the stranger be before the Lord" (Keritot 8b; below 5:1).

The process of the conversion of the people of Israel was not fully completed at the revelation at Mount Sinai, for even after the people of Israel as a whole converted through the Exodus from Egypt and the receiving of the Torah, very many souls belonging to Israel still remained scattered among the nations, and the completion of the rectification will be realized through their joining the people of Israel by individual conversion. As a result of the sin of Adam, good and evil and all values became intermingled with one another, and this included the souls of Israel becoming intermingled among the nations. And just as the overall process of clarifying good and evil and refining all values is complicated and prolonged, so the process of the souls of Israel returning to the rock from which they were hewn is complicated and prolonged; but without it the people of Israel will not be able to reveal faith and Torah in their full light, and will not be able to bring the full blessing to the world. Only after all of them return and convert will we merit the redemption through Mashiaḥ son of David, who himself is a descendant of two female converts (Yevamot 62a; Midrash Aggada, Bereishit 19:15; below section 12).4

sections.title: A Rectification for the Shattering of the Vessels
sections.html:
The masters of the esoteric tradition explained that even before God created this world, He created worlds that were destroyed, and they are called 'the World of Chaos' (Olam Ha-tohu). Their destruction occurred because the lights in them were too abundant, and the vessels were unable to contain them and shattered. As a result, the lights flew upward, and the fragments of the vessels, together with supernal sparks, descended and fell down into the abysses of evil. The lights are ideas and values, such as kindness, judgment and truth, and the vessels are the capacity to actualize them. And since the lights were too great, the vessels could not withstand them and shattered. They further explained that the main causes of their destruction were pride and separateness. Pride – for the lights took pride in their greatness, and instead of wrapping themselves in humility and shining into the vessels gently and gradually according to their limited capacity to receive, they shone into them with their full force until they shattered. Separateness – for each light sought to reign alone in the world. Kindness held that it was the important one and judgment must serve it, and judgment held that it was the important one and kindness must serve it. Had they taken each other into account, they would have moderated each other and shone with a blended light, and the vessels would have been able to receive their light and would not have shattered.

Upon the ruins of 'the World of Chaos' 'the World of Rectification' (Olam Ha-tikkun) was created, which is this world, whose creation is described in the Torah, and in which the rectification must be made for the destruction that occurred in 'the World of Chaos' at the time of 'the shattering of the vessels.' The rectification was to take place through the creation of a world in which values would appear in a balanced manner, as the Torah guides, and in which the lights would shine into the vessels with moderation according to the mitzvot of the Torah. In this way the vessels would gradually grow stronger and be able to receive more and more lights, and through them add life and blessing to the world, until they would be able to receive the great lights that were in 'the World of Chaos,' and redeem the holy sparks that fell into the abysses of evil at the time of the shattering of the vessels. But as a result of the sin of Adam, instead of the process of rectification beginning, parts of the good in the World of Rectification became intermingled with the evil of the World of Chaos, and parts of the evil in the World of Chaos became intermingled with the good of the World of Rectification; all the values became intermingled, and souls of Israel were scattered among the gentiles.

Granted, although the sin of Adam caused many grave complications whose rectification is long and painful, in the end the rectification will be greater and will raise the world to a higher level. Without the sin, the rectification would have been simple: all the values would have stood in their places and functioned properly, and from afar they would have raised up the sparks that fell in the shattering of the vessels, without expressing their full light. But as a result of the sin of Adam, souls of Israel were scattered among the gentiles, and they must return to the rock from which they were hewn in Israel through conversion. And every convert who returns brings up with him a holy spark that fell into the abysses of evil in the shattering of the vessels, and together with that spark he raises and elevates the good in the nation from which he sprang, thereby profoundly rectifying the sin of pride that was in 'the World of Chaos.' For in humility he joins Israel, and thereby returns the great lights of Chaos to their place.

In addition, through his conversion every convert also profoundly rectifies the sin of separateness. For the rectification and redemption of the world depend on the connection between Israel and the nations of the world; but without the sin, this connection would have existed from afar. After the sin, the connection between Israel and the nations did indeed become complex and complicated, painful and tormenting; but in the end, through the return of the souls of all the converts to Israel, the depth of the connection between Israel and the nations will be revealed. Through this more bridges and channels will be formed, through which Israel will be able to receive all the good in the nations, and as a result will be able to bestow more blessing and peace upon all the nations. By virtue of the converts who choose to join Israel, and by virtue of Israel who receive the converts with love, the complementary connection between Israel and the nations will be deeper and more fruitful, and the sin of separateness that caused 'the shattering of the vessels' will be more profoundly rectified, and faith will be revealed in a light doubled and redoubled, and goodness and blessing will increase without end.

sections.title: Avraham Our Father
sections.html:
Avraham our father is the father of Israel and also the father of converts. The father of Israel, as it is stated (Bereishit 12:1-3): "And the Lord said to Avram: Go forth from your land, from your birthplace and from your father's house, to the land that I will show you. And I will make you a great nation, and I will bless you and make your name great, and you shall be a blessing. And I will bless those who bless you, and him who curses you I will curse, and all the families of the earth shall be blessed through you." And the father of all converts, for Avraham our father would convert the men and Sara our mother would convert the women. And when they went up to the Land of Israel, they went up together with "the souls they had made in Ḥaran" (ibid. 12:5) – these are the converts whom they brought under the wings of the Divine Presence. They are called in the Torah "the souls they had made" to teach us that whoever draws a gentile near and converts him, Scripture regards him as though he had created and made him (Bereishit Rabba 39:14; Avot De-Rabbi Natan 12).

Avraham and Sara first engaged in converting converts, and through this they merited to be chosen to found the people of Israel. The Sages said (Avoda Zara 9a) that when Avraham our father reached the age of fifty-two, and the two thousand years of 'chaos' (tohu) of the world came to an end, Avraham and Sara began to convert converts, and thereby began the two thousand years of Torah. Only afterward, when Avraham our father was seventy-five years old, was he commanded to go up to the Land of Israel, and he received the tiding that a blessed nation would come forth from him. And only when he was a hundred years old was their son Yitzḥak born to him and Sara, the second father of Israel. Thus their work in conversion preceded the founding of the nation and the inheritance of the land.

Their devotion to bringing converts under the wings of the Divine Presence came from love of God and from love of humanity. Love of God – for out of their love for God they wished to make Him beloved by all people and to bring them under the wings of the Divine Presence. As it is stated (Devarim 6:5): "You shall love the Lord your God," and the Sages expounded: "Make Him beloved by people, as Avraham our father did" (Sifrei, ibid.). Their devotion to this also stemmed from love of humanity, in order to grant people the merit of Divine goodness and blessing.

The Sages said that by virtue of drawing converts near, Avraham our father merited to defeat the four mighty kings who had subdued the five kings of the Jordan plain and taken their people captive to sell them as slaves, and among them they had also taken captive Lot, his nephew. "The Holy One, blessed be He, said: I hold the convert so dear, and Avraham is the father of converts, and these wicked ones came to attack him (to make war on his relative) – woe to them, for their end is to fall before him" (Tanḥuma, Lekh Lekha 6).

Yitzḥak our father and Yaakov our father also continued in the ways of Avraham and converted converts (Bereishit Rabba 84:4). However, after they saw that many of the children of the converts whom Avraham and Sara had converted returned to their people and their religion, they did not convert as many as they had (Pri Tzaddik, Shemini 3). In any case, abundant blessing grew from all the converts whom the forefathers converted. First, because every additional person who merited the light of faith in God increased goodness and blessing for himself and for the whole world. Second, it is reasonable that the twelve sons of Yaakov our father married women from the daughters of the families that had converted; for this was the difference between Esav and Yaakov our father: Esav and his offspring married Canaanite women who worshiped idols, whereas Yaakov and his sons married women who had converted.5

sections.title: Ideal Conversions and After-the-Fact Conversions
sections.html:
Although, as a rule, the process of gathering in and converting the souls of Israel that were scattered among the gentiles is complex, it may take place with few difficulties, or it may be accompanied by many difficulties. It is possible that the conversions will take place in order to participate in the great destiny of the people of Israel to cleave to God, to His Torah and His mitzvot, and to bring blessing to the world, and then their absorption will be calm and joyful. And it is possible that they will convert and attach themselves to Israel out of material and spiritual hardships, and their absorption will involve halakhic, family and national complications.

The more the people of Israel cleave to God, to the Torah, to the mitzvot and to their destiny of bringing blessing to all the families of the earth, the more people are roused to convert for the sake of Heaven, and they hasten the coming of the redemption. And when Israel do not cleave to God and His Torah as they should, the process of converts joining is long, complicated and difficult, and Israel must go down into exile after exile among all the nations in order to absorb them. Granted, even when the people of Israel are at the low point of exile, there are righteous people who convert for the sake of Heaven. And the more Israel cleave to God even while in exile, the more of the converts convert for the sake of Heaven. But in practice, most converts converted out of complications of marital relationships and the like (Rambam, Hilkhot Issurei Bi'a 13:18). And since they did not convert for the sake of Heaven, many of them and of their descendants returned to their former ways and assimilated among the gentiles, and many others remained and caused Israel to sin; but in the end, in a painful and long process, their descendants integrated into Israel and contributed their special contribution, without which the people of Israel cannot advance toward its redemption.6

And so we find in the history of Israel that there were converts who converted for the sake of Heaven, such as Yitro, Raḥav and Onkelos the convert (below, chapter 2). On the other hand, many converts converted under pressure, and their conversion was accompanied by grave problems. For example, the Gibonim and the Samaritans (Kutim), who converted out of fear; therefore only some of their offspring merited to integrate into Israel, and most of them did not integrate into Israel, to the point that the Sages ruled not to intermarry with them – the Gibonim because they behaved with cruelty, not in the way of Israel (below 3:5-8), and the Samaritans because they continued to worship idols and obstructed the building of the Temple, and later even betrayed the Jews and allied themselves with the Romans who destroyed the Temple and the land. Yet halakhically they were still considered Jews, so that if they married a Jew, their marriage was valid (below 3:9-10).

Likewise, many conversions were carried out as a result of life's complications, such as manservants and maidservants who, when they were purchased, had to agree to accept the yoke of mitzvot through circumcision and immersion. And when they or their descendants were freed, they thereby became full Jews without the court having the ability to refuse to accept them (below 3:15-16). And there were women who joined the people of Israel as war captives according to the law of the 'beautiful captive woman' (eshet yefat to'ar). All these conversions, which were not done for the sake of Heaven, involved complications and suffering; but after all, blessing grew from them as well (below 3:17-18).

sections.title: The Difficulties in Accepting Converts
sections.html:
As we have learned, the less good the spiritual state of Israel, the more difficult and complicated the question of converts becomes. For many of those who seek to convert do not come for the sake of Heaven, and then a difficult problem confronts the judges (dayanim):

On the one hand, the Sages warned (Yevamot 24b) to accept converts who come to convert for the sake of Heaven, and not to accept those who come from ulterior motives, such as in order to marry a Jew. And they said (Yevamot 47b): "Converts are as hard for Israel as a sappaḥat, as it is stated (Yeshayahu 14:1): 'And the stranger shall join himself to them, and they shall cleave (ve-nispeḥu) to the house of Yaakov.'" A 'sappaḥat' is a skin lesion, which even when it is small is irritating and bothersome, but if it spreads, its damage grows. And since many converts did not observe Torah and mitzvot properly, many Israelites were drawn to behave as they did, to the point that the Sages said that they are as hard for Israel as a sappaḥat (Rashi and many Rishonim). Likewise the Rambam wrote that converts are as hard for Israel as the affliction of tzara'at, because most of them convert for the sake of some benefit and continue to sin and to cause Israel to sin, and it is difficult to separate from them after they have converted. Go and learn from what happened to Israel in the wilderness: the incident of the Golden Calf, Kivrot Ha-ta'ava and most of the trials occurred under the influence of the rabble, who are the 'mixed multitude' (Hilkhot Issurei Bi'a 13:18). Concerning those who accept such converts, the Sages said (Yevamot 109b): "Evil upon evil will come upon those who accept converts." This refers to those who persuade gentiles to convert, or who accept converts immediately without examining whether their intention is for the sake of Heaven (Tosafot, ibid.).7

On the other hand, the Sages ruled that after the fact (be-di'avad), if they converted converts who came for ulterior motives, such as for the sake of marriage, their conversion is valid (Yevamot 24b). Therefore, in pressing circumstances, in order to prevent assimilation, they converted in this manner as well (below 6:6). The Sages even warned not to push converts away too much, for "The Holy One, blessed be He, exiled Israel among the nations only so that converts would be added to them" (Pesaḥim 87b), and by pushing converts away one delays the redemption. The Sages likewise learned this from the story of Timna, who was a daughter of kings and wished to cleave to the offspring of Avraham our father and to convert. "She came to Avraham, Yitzḥak and Yaakov, and they did not accept her. She went and became a concubine to Elifaz son of Esav. She said: Better to be a maidservant to this nation than a mistress to another nation. From her came Amalek, who tormented Israel." From here the Sages learned that after Timna came back and asked again and again to convert, they should have converted her and not pushed her away (Sanhedrin 99b). Apparently the forefathers sensed that her character traits were not good, and feared that her children would be wicked, and therefore they did not want to convert her and marry her to one of those who would continue their line. But it turned out that this was a mistake, for since she came back and asked to convert, they should have accepted her (Masoret Ha-giyur 5:12-13).

Many times the reality is complex – for example, when the desire to convert began out of a relationship with a Jewish partner, but if the non-Jewish partner is not converted, there is concern that the Jew will assimilate and be lost to Israel. On the one hand, the convert's intention is not good enough, and it is likely that his conversion will cause troubles and complications, and some of his children will act wickedly and even return to assimilate among the gentiles. But on the other hand, by accepting him we increase the chance that his Jewish partner will remain connected to Judaism and not assimilate among the nations, and there is even a chance that their children will take root in Israel, and from them will emerge great and righteous people who will add blessing to the world. In such situations some tend to convert and some tend to reject, and many times the matter depends on the character and the soul-root of the judge, as in the case of Shammai, who tended to push away, and Hillel, who tended to draw near (below 4:6).

sections.title: Exile and Redemption Depend on Conversion
sections.html:
The future redemption depends on the gathering in of all the souls of the converts, because each soul has its own special virtue, and as long as its special light has not been revealed, the redemption is delayed. As the Sages said (Yevamot 62a): "The son of David will not come until all the souls in the guf are exhausted, as it is stated (Yeshayahu 57:16): 'For I will not contend forever, nor will I be angry eternally, for the spirit that enwraps itself is from Me, and the souls I have made.'" The meaning of the 'guf' here is the treasury of the souls of Israel while they are still in a raw state, before their descent into the world and before they have shed their light. And God said that He will not contend with Israel forever, nor be angry with the world eternally; rather, there are spirits and souls, and after all the souls of Israel have revealed their special light over the course of the generations, the redemption will come. And even if the general state of that generation is bad, God will combine all the rectifications of all the souls from all the generations, and will bring redemption through Mashiaḥ son of David.

That is to say, it is possible that the redemption will come through repentance that will rouse all of Israel to reveal their light, and as a result all the converts as well will be roused to return to the source from which they were hewn. This is the redemption of 'I will hasten it' (aḥishena), which comes calmly, joyfully and speedily. Granted, even if Israel do not repent properly, the redemption will come in the end, but it will come with harsh and terrible sufferings that will last for generations, and this is the redemption of 'in its time' (be-itah) (Sanhedrin 97b; Peninei Halakha, Zemanim 4, note 2). For all the good ideas and deeds of Israel, without exception, are never lost. And every Jew, even if he is wicked, reveals in his life, through suffering, good points from the root of his soul. And so in a long and painful process, Israel reveal all the good ideas and deeds at the root of their souls, and through the sufferings of the exiles all the souls of the converts, too, return by various and strange paths to the rock from which they were hewn – until all the good ideas and deeds of Israel and of the converts from all the generations are combined, and the redemption comes.

But as long as there is a soul of a convert that has not yet joined Israel, its special light cannot be revealed, and the redemption is delayed. As the Sages said (Pesaḥim 87b): "The Holy One, blessed be He, exiled Israel among the nations only so that converts would be added to them," as it is stated (Hoshea 2:25): "And I will sow her for Myself in the land, and I will have compassion on Lo-Ruḥama, and I will say to Lo-Ammi: You are My people, and he shall say: My God." The Sages explained: "'And I will sow her for Myself in the land' – does a person sow a se'a except to bring in several kor?" That is, a person sows in order to grow a quantity many times greater than what was sown (a kor is 30 se'a). Therefore "Israel are dispersed in all the lands more than the other nations, so that converts will be added to them" (Tosafot, Kiddushin 70b, s.v. "kashim"). And although many times these converts convert out of after-the-fact situations, they too will be considered God's people, as it is stated: "and I will say to Lo-Ammi: You are My people, and he shall say: My God," and each one of them will add his special light.

Ideally, the process of absorbing converts should take place by virtue of Israel dwelling in their land, meriting great blessing and sanctifying the name of Heaven through their good deeds. And out of appreciation for the truth and goodness that Israel radiate, converts from all the nations will desire to walk in their ways, and will be roused to return to the source from which they were hewn and will convert. And when Israel sin, Israel must go down into exile, and in a complex and painful process they reveal their devotion to the faith and gather in the souls of all the converts. Rut the Moabite, too, joined Israel as a consequence of sins and complications, until she rose to greatness through her kindness, and by her merit the royal dynasty in Israel was continued, for she is the great-grandmother of King David, and from her descendants will come Mashiaḥ son of David (below 2:5).

The future of the conversion depends to a large extent on the way the convert is received. For even if he converted without pure intention, if he is received with respect and a welcoming countenance, the chance increases that he will integrate into Israel and rise in the observance of Torah and mitzvot. Therefore it is fitting for us to strengthen ourselves in the mitzvot of the Torah to love the convert with an especially great love and to honor him, and to take great care not to cause him distress; and thereby we will merit a double reward. First, through our moral conduct itself we will merit to rise in the virtues of Torah and mitzvot. Second, by virtue of receiving converts with love and respect, the converts will integrate properly into Israel and will contribute their full contribution to the redemption of Israel and the world.
